claims.text: The starting material is an as-synthesized, random, equiatomic transition-metal high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous but chemically disordered distribution of transition-metal atoms.
Configurational disorder creates local variations in electron density.
Disorder-induced electron-density variations enhance electron–phonon coupling in selected regions.
The locally enhanced electron–phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation in a dirty-limit state.
Targeted annealing or slight compositional tuning can introduce controlled local chemical ordering and modulate configurational entropy.
The relevant superconducting test regime is below approximately 10 K at ambient pressure.
Local fluctuations in chemical arrangement mediate variations in the local electronic density of states and pairing potential.
The interplay of chemical disorder and electron–phonon coupling creates regions with enhanced pairing interactions.
Increasing local chemical order reduces electronic scattering in favorable regions.
Reduced scattering allows superconducting domains to percolate.
Partial local chemical ordering will raise the superconducting transition temperature relative to the untreated disordered state.
Partial local chemical ordering will produce a sharper superconducting transition relative to the untreated state.
The proposed mechanism applies to transition-metal HEAs whose superconductivity is in the dirty-limit regime.
The ordering effect becomes less pronounced when disorder exceeds an optimal range.
The ordering effect becomes less pronounced at temperatures where thermal fluctuations dominate electron–phonon effects.

Failure of the ordered sample to show any statistically significant improvement in Tc, transition sharpness, or critical current density relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
